title: OpenSandbox: Give an AI Agent a Safe Workshop
summary: Follow one request to run python main.py from an agent, through OpenSandbox, into an isolated runtime, and back as streamed output.
audience: curious developer who is new to sandbox infrastructure

truthLadder.analogy: OpenSandbox is like a workshop manager: it prepares a separate workroom, hands the job through a controlled door, and closes the room when the booking ends.
truthLadder.mechanism: OpenSandbox combines SDKs, CLI and MCP entry points, public API contracts, a lifecycle control plane, Docker or Kubernetes runtime backends, and an in-sandbox execd daemon for commands, files, code, metrics, and streamed output.
truthLadder.caveat: OpenSandbox is not a magic security boundary by itself. Actual isolation depends on the configured runtime, network policy, credentials, volumes, resource limits, and operator choices; standard runc is not the same protection as gVisor, Kata, or Firecracker-backed isolation.

scenes.title: A separate place for risky work
scenes.question: Why give an AI agent a sandbox at all?
scenes.simpleAnswer: Because generated code should get its own workroom instead of free access to your main machine.
scenes.technicalAnswer: OpenSandbox gives applications a uniform way to create time- and resource-bounded environments, run commands or code, move files, expose services, and then terminate the environment.
scenes.caveat: A sandbox reduces blast radius; it does not make arbitrary code harmless or replace careful configuration and monitoring.
scenes.takeaway: Put risky execution behind a deliberate boundary.

scenes.title: The manager is not the room
scenes.question: Is OpenSandbox just Docker with a nicer name?
scenes.simpleAnswer: No. Docker can be one kind of room; OpenSandbox is the common desk that knows how to manage rooms.
scenes.technicalAnswer: OpenSandbox defines runtime-neutral APIs and clients, while its lifecycle server selects one backend implementation: Docker for local or single-host use, or Kubernetes through a supported workload provider.
scenes.caveat: The shared API hides many platform details, but Docker and Kubernetes still differ in endpoint routing, storage, pause/resume behavior, and deployment complexity.
scenes.takeaway: OpenSandbox is a protocol and control layer over runtime backends.

scenes.title: Creating the workroom
scenes.question: How does a new sandbox actually appear?
scenes.simpleAnswer: The client asks; the server checks the request; a runtime builds the room and reports when it is ready.
scenes.technicalAnswer: A create call reaches POST /v1/sandboxes. The FastAPI lifecycle server validates it, delegates to Docker or Kubernetes, stages execd plus optional volume and egress configuration, and exposes an asynchronous state that clients poll until Running or Failed.
scenes.caveat: Create is asynchronous. Receiving a sandbox ID is not proof that the workload is already ready.
scenes.takeaway: Creation is an orchestrated state transition, not an instant function call.

scenes.title: The controlled door inside
scenes.question: How does python main.py run inside?
scenes.simpleAnswer: The client finds a controlled door called execd, sends the command through it, and receives live output.
scenes.technicalAnswer: The client resolves execd's sandbox endpoint or uses the server proxy, authenticates when required, then calls execd. Execd starts the process and streams status, stdout, stderr, results, and completion events over SSE; interactive PTY sessions use WebSockets.
scenes.caveat: The lifecycle server creates and locates sandboxes; execd owns operations inside the sandbox. Mixing those roles makes the architecture harder to secure and debug.
scenes.takeaway: The control plane finds the room; execd does the work inside it.

scenes.title: Several guards, not one magic wall
scenes.question: What stops the code from wandering everywhere?
scenes.simpleAnswer: Several guards work together: the runtime boundary, resource limits, network rules, endpoint access, and careful credentials.
scenes.technicalAnswer: The runtime can apply container or stronger secure-runtime isolation; OpenSandbox can add resource limits, capability and policy controls, an egress sidecar, ingress routing with secure endpoint headers, and Credential Vault-based outbound credential injection.
scenes.caveat: These protections are deployment choices. The default runc path is useful for trusted local development but is not equivalent to a user-space kernel or VM-backed runtime for hostile multi-tenant code.
scenes.takeaway: Security is a configured stack of boundaries.

scenes.title: End the room; keep only what you mean to keep
scenes.question: What ends, and what can survive?
scenes.simpleAnswer: The workroom can pause, resume, expire, or be deleted; durable data survives only through an intentional storage path.
scenes.technicalAnswer: The lifecycle API exposes Pending, Running, pause/resume transitions, stopping and terminal states, plus Failed. Volumes use runtime-neutral models, while snapshots and pause/resume semantics differ between Docker and Kubernetes implementations.
scenes.caveat: Do not assume a paused sandbox, deleted sandbox, mounted volume, and snapshot mean the same thing. Docker and Kubernetes materialize persistence and recovery differently.
scenes.takeaway: Treat cleanup and persistence as explicit lifecycle decisions.

teachBack.question: Why is OpenSandbox more than a Docker wrapper?
options: It defines common clients and APIs while delegating to Docker or Kubernetes backends
It replaces every container with the same virtual machine
It runs the AI model inside the lifecycle server
teachBack.explanation: The important split is contract and orchestration versus platform-specific execution. Docker is one backend, not the whole system.

teachBack.question: Who actually runs python main.py inside the sandbox?
options: The injected execd daemon starts it and streams the result
The public OpenAPI file executes it directly
The ingress gateway rewrites it into a container image
teachBack.explanation: The lifecycle plane creates and locates the sandbox; execd owns commands, files, sessions, code, and metrics inside it.

teachBack.question: Why is enabling OpenSandbox not enough to guarantee strong isolation?
options: Protection depends on the configured runtime, network, credentials, mounts, and limits
Every sandbox automatically uses a Firecracker microVM
Streaming stdout bypasses all runtime boundaries
teachBack.explanation: Security comes from a configured stack. Standard containers, gVisor, and VM-backed runtimes provide different boundaries, and policy choices still matter.

teachBack.question: What should a client do after receiving a new sandbox ID?
options: Poll state or use a readiness helper until Running or Failed
Assume the first command already finished
Delete the sandbox so execd can start
teachBack.explanation: Creation is asynchronous. An ID means the request exists, not necessarily that the workload is ready.
